text: For an athlete entering a new training block, validity asks whether a test measures:
options: The intended construct or performance quality
The stability of the score across repeated trials
The test's ability to detect a true case
The degree to which trained raters agree
explanation: Validity concerns whether the test supports the intended interpretation and use of its score.

text: A 20-m sprint test is intended to represent acceleration. Which finding most directly supports its criterion validity?
options: Its scores are similar when repeated after 48 hours with the same protocol
Two assessors obtain similar stopwatch readings on the same task
Its instructions are easy for athletes to understand with the same protocol
Its scores are associated with an established acceleration measure
explanation: Because criterion validity compares the new 20-m sprint with an established acceleration measure, an association between their scores supports the intended acceleration interpretation.

text: A jump test gives stable values but does not reflect lower-body power. This test is best described as:
options: Valid and reliable for lower-body power
Sensitive but not specific for lower-body power
Specific but not standardized for lower-body power
Reliable but not valid for the intended construct
explanation: Stable values show repeatability, but failure to reflect lower-body power means validity for that intended construct is not established.

text: To support the content validity of a soccer fitness battery, the selected tasks should:
options: Use the least expensive equipment in the facility
Use one familiar laboratory test for every player
Copy a battery designed for another sport
Sample the physical qualities required in soccer
explanation: Content validity is supported when the battery samples the physical qualities required for soccer performance.

text: A rehabilitation team wants to interpret a hop test as a readiness measure. Before doing so, it should establish that:
options: The test has a short administration time
Evidence supports the readiness interpretation
The score is normally distributed in every athlete
The test uses the same footwear in all sports
explanation: A hop score should be interpreted as readiness only when evidence supports that readiness interpretation, not merely because the test is quick or familiar.

text: Which observation would most strongly support construct validity for a balance test?
options: The assessor completes the form quickly
The athlete receives identical instructions twice
The device reports values to one decimal place
Scores relate to established balance measures
explanation: Construct validity is supported when balance scores relate to established measures of balance.

text: A test is proposed to measure repeated-sprint ability. Which result would question its validity?
options: Its score is unrelated to established sprint measures
Its scores vary slightly across repeated standardized sessions
It requires a standardized warm-up before each trial
It has a clearly defined stopping rule for testing
explanation: If the score is unrelated to established sprint measures, the result questions whether the test captures repeated-sprint ability.

text: When a new agility test is compared with an accepted agility test in the same athletes, the comparison primarily examines:
options: Inter-rater reliability
Test administration feasibility
Criterion-related validity
The smallest worthwhile change
explanation: Comparing the new agility test with an accepted agility measure in the same athletes examines criterion-related validity.

text: Test–retest reliability refers most directly to the:
options: Consistency of scores under repeated conditions
Agreement with the intended construct being measured
Detection of true cases during a screening test
Agreement between independent trained raters
explanation: Test–retest reliability is the consistency or repeatability of scores when the same measurement is repeated under stable conditions.

text: A goalkeeper completes the same reaction-time test twice under unchanged conditions. The most relevant reliability question is whether:
options: The test predicts the next match result
The assessor agrees with the coach’s selection view
The test detects every athlete with an injury
Repeated sessions produce similar scores
explanation: With conditions unchanged, similar reaction-time scores across sessions support test–retest reliability.

text: A second trial is much faster because an athlete has become familiar with the task. This mainly threatens:
options: Construct validity of the reference standard
Test–retest reliability through a practice effect
Specificity of an injury-screening threshold
The ecological validity of a laboratory measure
explanation: The practice effect changes the second score without a corresponding performance change, reducing repeatability and therefore test–retest reliability.

text: To estimate random error in a stable field test, the practitioner should:
options: Compare the score only with a national ranking
Change the surface between every administration
Repeat the standardized test and quantify typical error
Select the highest score as the athlete’s true value
explanation: Repeating the standardized test permits estimation of typical error rather than treating the highest score as the athlete’s true value.

text: Two physiotherapists score the same movement video independently. This design primarily assesses:
options: Test–retest reliability
Criterion validity
Sensitivity to change
Inter-rater reliability
explanation: Inter-rater reliability is the agreement or consistency of scores assigned independently by different raters assessing the same performance or material.

text: For a stable athlete, a reliable monitoring measure should show:
options: A different score whenever the coach changes the target
A high value only during competition under stable conditions
Small random variation when repeated under the same conditions
Perfect agreement with every physiological variable
explanation: Small random variation under identical conditions is expected in a reliable measure; perfect agreement with every physiological variable is not required.

text: An athlete’s second score exceeds the typical error of the test while preparation was unchanged. The change is more likely to represent:
options: A difference caused by assessor disagreement
A real change beyond measurement noise
A loss of construct validity in the test
A false-positive screening classification
explanation: A change larger than typical error is less likely to be measurement noise, although practical importance still requires a decision threshold.

text: Which conclusion cannot be made from high test–retest reliability alone?
options: The test necessarily measures the intended construct
Scores are repeatable under the tested conditions
Measurement error may be acceptably small
The protocol should be kept stable across sessions
explanation: Reliability shows repeatability, not that the test measures the intended construct; validity evidence is still needed.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, sensitivity of a screening test is the ability to identify:
options: People who truly have the target condition
People who truly lack the target condition
People whose score falls below a performance norm
People who report symptoms without a confirmed condition
explanation: Sensitivity is the proportion of true cases correctly identified by a test.

text: A screen identifies 18 of 20 athletes who truly have the target condition. Its sensitivity is:
explanation: Sensitivity is the proportion of true cases detected: 18 of 20 cases gives 18/20 = 90%.

text: In a screening programme, a false negative is an athlete who:
options: Does not have the condition but tests positive
Has an abnormal performance score but no diagnosis
Has the condition but tests negative
Declines testing after receiving information
explanation: A false negative occurs when an athlete has the target condition but receives a negative test result.

text: When missing a dangerous condition would be unacceptable, the initial screening test should generally prioritize:
options: A high specificity to minimize false positives
A high sensitivity to minimize missed cases
A low sensitivity to reduce referral numbers
A normative percentile rather than a diagnostic reference
explanation: When missing a dangerous condition is unacceptable, high sensitivity reduces missed true cases, even if false positives increase.

text: Among 50 athletes known to have an injury risk condition, 45 screen positive. Which quantity has been calculated?
options: Specificity
Sensitivity
Positive predictive value
Negative predictive value
explanation: Sensitivity uses confirmed cases as the denominator: 45 positive screens among 50 cases gives 45/50 = 90%.

text: A screening tool has low sensitivity. The main concern is that it will:
options: Classify many healthy athletes as positive cases
Agree perfectly with a reference standard
Miss many athletes who have the condition
Require no follow-up assessment after screening
explanation: Low sensitivity means the screen fails to identify a larger proportion of athletes who truly have the condition.

text: Sensitivity must be estimated using which denominator?
options: All athletes with a positive test result
All athletes who report any symptom
All athletes with the confirmed condition
All athletes who complete the protocol
explanation: Sensitivity is calculated among all athletes with the confirmed condition, not among all positive tests or all tested athletes.

text: If a screening threshold is lowered so that more athletes test positive, sensitivity will often:
options: Increase, although specificity may decrease
Fall because more false negatives are created
Remain fixed regardless of the threshold
Become identical to positive predictive value
explanation: Lowering the threshold usually captures more true cases and raises sensitivity, while potentially reducing specificity.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, specificity of a screening test is the ability to identify:
options: People who truly lack the target condition
People who truly have the target condition
People whose score falls below a performance norm
People who test negative without knowing true status
explanation: Specificity is the ability to classify people who truly lack the target condition as negative.

text: A screening test is negative in 92 of 100 athletes who are confirmed not to have the condition. Its specificity is:
explanation: Specificity is the proportion of confirmed non-cases testing negative: 92 of 100 gives 92%.

text: A confirmatory test is chosen after an initial positive screen. High specificity is useful because it:
options: Maximizes the number of missed cases
Removes the need for a reference standard
Reduces false-positive classifications
Ensures that every positive result predicts injury
explanation: A high-specificity confirmatory test limits false-positive classifications among people who do not have the condition.

text: Specificity is the proportion of:
options: True cases with positive results
True non-cases with negative results
All positive results that are true cases
All negative results from true non-cases
explanation: Specificity counts true non-cases that receive negative results.

text: A test with high specificity can still have poor sensitivity. This means it may:
options: Create very few false positives among non-cases
Miss true cases despite clearing many non-cases
Measure performance rather than classification accuracy
Remain valid for every screening purpose
explanation: High specificity can coexist with poor sensitivity, so the test may miss true cases while correctly clearing many non-cases.

text: If specificity is 85%, the false-positive rate is:
explanation: The false-positive rate is 1 − specificity: 1 − 0.85 = 0.15, or 15%.

text: A stricter positive threshold for an injury screen will often:
options: Increase sensitivity and lower specificity
Increase specificity and may lower sensitivity
Leave both sensitivity and specificity unchanged
Convert predictive value into reliability
explanation: A stricter positive threshold generally reduces false positives and raises specificity, but may miss more true cases and lower sensitivity.

text: After a broad screen identifies possible exertional risk, the follow-up test should generally emphasize:
options: Maximum sensitivity regardless of false positives
Specificity to confirm the condition among positives
A generic performance ranking among non-cases
A different outcome unrelated to the initial concern
explanation: After a broad screen, a specific follow-up test helps confirm the condition among athletes who screened positive.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a sport-specific test battery should be selected mainly according to:
options: Sport demands, athlete level, purpose, and test evidence
The laboratory equipment, staff time, budget, and convenience
A single generic normative table used across all athletes
A familiar battery used with a different sport and population
explanation: Test selection should reflect the performance question, sport demands, athlete characteristics, and evidence.

text: A volleyball battery is being planned for a national-level squad. Which combination best reflects its sport demands?
options: Repeated-jump ability, short sprinting, and change-of-direction tasks
Only a long-distance endurance test and resting heart rate
A generic battery selected without regard to playing position
A laboratory test chosen solely because its equipment is available
explanation: A volleyball battery should sample repeated jumping, short sprinting, and change-of-direction demands that occur in the sport.

text: For return-to-play testing after an ankle injury, the battery should first be chosen to:
options: Maximize the number of tests despite fatigue
Use the athlete’s preferred pre-injury exercise
Measure safe functions relevant to return decisions
Replace clinical examination with one score
explanation: Return-to-play testing should measure safe, sport-relevant functions that inform the return decision rather than replace clinical examination.

text: A coach requests one battery for sprinters and marathoners. The best response is to:
options: Use the same tests because all athletes need identical norms
Tailor tests to the distinct demands and athlete groups
Select the battery by the available stopwatch only
Choose the tests that produce the highest scores
explanation: Sprinters and marathoners have different performance demands, so their test batteries should be tailored to their groups.

text: A testing battery is too long to complete without fatigue affecting later tests. The most defensible revision is to:
options: Keep every test and ignore order effects
Remove every test with a numerical outcome
Retain relevant tests; shorten the battery
Replace safety screening with extra performance trials
explanation: If battery length creates fatigue, retaining the relevant tests and shortening the battery protects interpretability of later results.

text: When selecting tests for a youth development squad, the practitioner should give particular weight to:
options: Apply adult elite norms without adjustment to maturation
Use the most fatiguing maximal protocol available to adults
Prioritize age-appropriate safety and relevant qualities
Use equipment unavailable to the youth programme
explanation: Youth testing should prioritize age-appropriate safety and relevant qualities rather than applying adult maximal protocols without adjustment.

text: A field battery is intended to guide weekly training. Which feature makes it most useful?
options: Produce a ranking that cannot be repeated
Be valid, reliable, feasible, and decision-relevant
Use maximal effort for every physical quality measured
Avoid recording preparation and environment
explanation: A battery guiding weekly training must be valid, reliable, feasible, and connected to the decision it is intended to support.

text: Two possible batteries measure similar qualities. The preferred battery is the one that:
options: Have the most equipment and longest testing time
Use the highest available normative reference values
Match the purpose while limiting unnecessary burden
Use a familiar battery from another population
explanation: When batteries measure similar qualities, the better choice matches the purpose while limiting unnecessary time and athlete burden.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, normative data are most useful when the reference group is:
options: Comparable in age, sex, sport, level, and setting
Comparable in age and sport, but tested differently
A larger group with limited demographic information
A high-performing subgroup from the same sport only
explanation: Normative values are most interpretable when the reference group matches the athlete and testing setting in the relevant characteristics.

text: A 16-year-old middle-distance runner is compared with a published reference group. Interpretation is strongest when the group matches the runner’s:
options: Event only, regardless of maturation and protocol
Personal best only, without a reference distribution
Coach’s preferred ranking system for this comparison
Age, sex, event, performance level, and test conditions
explanation: The comparison is strongest when the reference group matches the runner’s age, sex, event, performance level, and test conditions.

text: An athlete’s z-score is −1.0 on a test using an appropriate reference sample. This means the athlete scored:
options: One raw unit below the test minimum
One percentile below the reference median
One standard deviation below the reference mean
One standard error above the reference mean
explanation: A z-score of −1.0 means the result is one standard deviation below the reference mean.

text: Normative values collected on a different protocol should not be used directly because:
options: A larger sample always produces biased test scores
Percentiles cannot be calculated for athletes
Norms apply only to laboratory variables
Different protocols can change performance
explanation: Different protocols can change the measured performance, so values collected under another protocol may not be directly comparable.

text: A youth athlete is being compared with elite adult norms. The main interpretation problem is:
options: Elite adult groups always have lower measurement error
Youth athletes cannot complete field tests
Maturation and level may make norms inappropriate
Adult norms are always criterion-referenced
explanation: Differences in maturation and performance level can make elite adult norms inappropriate for a youth athlete.

text: For a higher-is-better measure, an athlete at the 75th percentile had a score above:
options: Exactly 75% of every athlete in the sport for this comparison
Only the athletes who trained during the same week for this comparison
Approximately three quarters of the reference group on that measure
All athletes outside the reference population for this comparison
explanation: The 75th percentile indicates a score approximately as high as or higher than three quarters of the relevant reference group.

text: Normative data are best used to:
options: Describe how an athlete compares with a relevant reference group
Diagnose an injury without clinical assessment for this comparison
Replace repeated testing and individual baseline values
Prove that an athlete will win a competition for this comparison
explanation: Normative data describe an athlete’s position relative to a relevant reference group; they do not diagnose injury or guarantee competition results.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a principal advantage of field testing is that it:
options: Provides laboratory precision for every variable
Removes environmental effects from field performance
Needs no standardization across sessions
Reflects sport conditions with portable resources
explanation: Field tests can be practical and ecologically relevant, although control and measurement precision may be lower.

text: A rugby team wants to monitor repeated sprint ability on its normal training pitch. The chief advantage of a field test is that it:
options: Eliminates all weather and surface effects
Provides laboratory precision for every variable
Reflects sport demands in a practical setting
Requires no standardized timing or instructions
explanation: A repeated-sprint field test on the normal pitch can represent sport demands while remaining practical for team monitoring.

text: A limitation of a field test conducted outdoors after rainfall is that:
options: It cannot measure any performance outcome in field testing
It automatically has higher validity than a laboratory test
It removes the need for an athlete warm-up in field testing
Surface and environmental variation may reduce comparability
explanation: Rainfall can alter surface and environmental conditions, reducing comparability between outdoor field-test sessions.

text: A large academy has limited laboratory access but needs a frequent readiness measure. A field test is attractive mainly because it:
options: Measures every physiological mechanism directly
Can test many athletes with portable equipment
Makes standardization unnecessary in field testing
Guarantees scores are free of fatigue effects
explanation: Portable field equipment permits frequent testing of many athletes when laboratory access is limited.

text: To improve the interpretability of a 30-m sprint performed on a field, the team should:
options: Allow each athlete to select a different surface in field testing
Keep surface, start, timing, footwear, and instructions consistent
Change the timing device between sessions in field testing
Record only the fastest athlete’s result in field testing
explanation: Consistent surface, start, timing, footwear, and instructions reduce avoidable variation in the 30-m field sprint.

text: A coach asks whether a field test can reflect match demands. The best answer is that field testing:
options: Can reflect sport demands when the task is representative
Is valid only when performed in a laboratory
Is automatically more reliable than laboratory testing
Measures performance independently of motivation and pacing
explanation: A field test can reflect match demands when its task is representative of the sport, although motivation and conditions still require control.

text: If the question concerns precise oxygen uptake under controlled conditions, a field test may be less suitable because it:
options: Cannot be performed by trained athletes in ordinary outdoor conditions
Always has poorer construct validity than laboratory tests
Cannot be standardized under ordinary outdoor field conditions
Usually provides less control and direct physiological measurement
explanation: For precise oxygen uptake, field testing usually offers less environmental control and less direct physiological measurement than a laboratory protocol.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a laboratory test is particularly useful when the goal is to:
options: Maximize ecological validity under normal competition conditions
Eliminate the need for standardized preparation and safety screening
Control conditions and quantify a physiological variable
Estimate sport performance without controlling the variable
explanation: Laboratories can provide controlled conditions and specialized measurement, but practical relevance must still be considered.

text: A laboratory treadmill test is preferred when the practitioner needs to:
options: Reproduce a normal match environment exactly
Avoid all screening and emergency preparation
Control workload while measuring gas exchange
Rank athletes without defining the physiological variable
explanation: A laboratory test is useful when controlled conditions and direct quantification of a physiological variable are the primary goals.

text: A researcher studying lactate response chooses a laboratory protocol primarily to:
options: Remove the need for repeated measurements
Control speed, grade, sampling, and timing
Make results independent of exercise mode
Guarantee lactate predicts competition performance
explanation: A treadmill permits controlled workload progression while the metabolic cart measures gas exchange.

text: One trade-off of a laboratory cycling test compared with a sport-specific field test is that it may have lower:
options: Measurement precision in a laboratory protocol
Ecological validity for the athlete’s sport
Safety screening requirements with the same protocol
Ability to control workload in a laboratory protocol
explanation: The laboratory protocol controls workload and measurement, but may be less representative of the athlete’s sport and therefore have lower ecological validity.

text: A laboratory assessment of maximal oxygen uptake should include which preparation?
options: Use a standard pre-test routine and safety screen
Exercise without preparation immediately beforehand
Change equipment at each stage to increase realism
Continue despite a recognized contraindication
explanation: A standard pre-test routine and safety screen help make maximal oxygen-uptake testing comparable and safe.

text: A sports scientist uses a controlled ramp test to compare two training phases. The main methodological benefit is:
options: The athlete’s motivation is no longer relevant
The same workload progression can be reproduced
The outcome automatically becomes sport-specific
One trial is sufficient to establish a baseline
explanation: A controlled ramp test allows the same workload progression to be reproduced when two training phases are compared.

text: When a laboratory and field test produce different results, the practitioner should first ask whether they:
options: Use the same normative percentile table
Compare the same protocol across both settings
Compare equipment costs for both tests
Measure the same outcome in similar conditions
explanation: Different results should first be interpreted by checking whether the tests measure the same outcome under similar conditions.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a test-retest change should be interpreted against:
options: The athlete's ranking, position, and recent performance
The typical error and smallest worthwhile change
Only the direction of the observed change
A universal percentage applied to every test
explanation: A test–retest change should be judged against typical error and the smallest worthwhile change, not its direction alone.

text: An athlete’s 20-m sprint improves by 0.02 s, while the test’s typical error is 0.04 s. The result should be described as:
options: Clearly larger than measurement error
Smaller than the expected measurement error
Proof of a meaningful training adaptation
Equivalent to a one-standard-deviation gain
explanation: The 0.02-second improvement is smaller than the 0.04-second typical error, so it is not clearly beyond expected measurement noise.

text: The smallest worthwhile change is useful because it helps the practitioner judge whether a change is:
options: Large enough to matter for the performance decision
Statistically impossible in a single athlete
Independent of the test’s measurement error
Identical for every athlete and every test
explanation: The smallest worthwhile change helps determine whether an observed change is large enough to alter the performance decision.

text: For a repeated jump test, the most defensible longitudinal comparison uses:
options: Use the same protocol and similar preparation
Use a new device at every session
Keep only the athlete’s best historical score
Apply one percentage rule to every test
explanation: Using the same protocol and similar preparation makes repeated jump scores more defensible as a longitudinal comparison.

text: A test is responsive when it can:
options: Produce a high score in every athlete tested
Replace a reference standard during diagnosis
Detect meaningful change when performance changes
Eliminate all biological variation in testing
explanation: A responsive test detects meaningful performance change when the athlete’s performance genuinely changes.

text: An athlete improves beyond typical error but not beyond the pre-specified smallest worthwhile change. The appropriate conclusion is:
options: The change is statistically and practically decisive
The test has no reliability because the score changed
The change may be real, but practical importance is uncertain
The athlete must have worsened despite the higher score
explanation: Exceeding typical error suggests the change may be real, but failing to exceed the pre-specified worthwhile change leaves its practical importance uncertain.

text: Why is a universal 5% improvement rule problematic across different tests?
options: All tests have exactly 5% measurement error in this athlete
Percentage change cannot be calculated for performance data
Tests differ in scale, error, variability, and practical importance
Normative data always make percentage change invalid
explanation: A universal percentage rule ignores differences in test scale, measurement error, variability, and the practical importance of change; interpretation should account for the test's measurement properties and meaningfulness.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, why is test sequencing important in an athlete assessment battery?
options: Fatiguing tests can influence later results
Always place less-fatiguing tests after maximal tests
Fixed order leaves later effort unchanged
Normative scores remain comparable despite fatigue
explanation: Fatigue, potentiation, and psychological effects can alter later test performance, so sequence should be planned.

text: In a battery containing a countermovement jump and a 3-km run, which sequence best limits fatigue effects on power?
options: 3-km run before the jump
Alternate randomly for each athlete
Jump before the endurance test
Perform both simultaneously
explanation: The 3-km run can induce fatigue and reduce subsequent jump performance, so placing the countermovement jump first limits fatigue carryover into the power measure.

text: During a physiological battery, resting heart rate and blood pressure should generally be recorded:
options: After the maximal test in the battery
Before exercise, after an appropriate quiet rest
Only if the athlete reports fatigue afterward
At a different time for every participant
explanation: Resting heart rate and blood pressure should be recorded before exercise after a quiet rest period, because acute exercise and fatigue can raise or otherwise alter these measures; allowing rest helps reduce the influence of the preceding activity and establishes a comparable resting baseline.

text: A protocol includes three maximal sprint trials. To reduce carryover, the team should:
options: Remove recovery periods to equalize discomfort in the battery
Let each athlete choose a different trial duration with the same protocol
Use the fastest first trial as the final score in the battery
Provide a defined recovery interval and consistent encouragement
explanation: Defined recovery intervals and consistent encouragement reduce fatigue, potentiation, and motivational differences between maximal sprint trials.

text: Why should a familiarization trial precede a formal technical test?
options: It removes the need for a valid outcome measure in the battery
It guarantees that every athlete reaches maximal effort
It reduces learning effects that could distort the formal score
It makes environmental conditions irrelevant in the battery
explanation: Familiarization reduces learning effects, so the formal technical score is less likely to reflect task novelty.

text: When two tests use the same muscle groups, the order should be planned mainly to:
options: Maximize fatigue before the most important measure
Minimize fatigue and potentiation affecting later results
Ensure that the last test always has the highest score
Make all tests last exactly the same time in the battery
explanation: Planning the order of tests minimizes fatigue and potentiation from earlier tests affecting later results.

text: A balance score falls sharply when measured immediately after exhaustive intervals. The most likely explanation is:
options: The reference group changed between sessions
Fatigue influenced the later balance assessment
The balance test became more valid after fatigue
The stopwatch measured specificity instead
explanation: Exhaustive intervals can temporarily impair balance, so fatigue is the most direct explanation for the later lower score.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, the main purpose of an SOP in sports-science testing is to:
options: Allow each tester to alter the protocol according to preference
Replace consent and safety screening with written instructions
Guarantee higher scores by making the testing routine familiar
Standardize procedures for consistent interpretation across sessions
explanation: A standard operating procedure reduces procedural variation and supports repeatable data collection.

text: An SOP for a repeated sprint test should state:
options: Only the name of the assessor in the SOP
The athlete’s expected ranking before testing
Preparation, equipment, scoring, and safety steps
A different warm-up for each testing session
explanation: An SOP should specify preparation, equipment, scoring, and safety so repeated sprint testing is performed consistently and safely.

text: An assessor changes the recovery interval because the facility is delayed. The correct quality-control action is to:
options: Document the deviation and assess its impact
Hide the deviation so the dataset is complete
Delete the athlete’s previous scores
Change the score to match the protocol target
explanation: Changing the recovery interval is a protocol deviation; documenting it allows its effect on interpretation to be assessed.

text: Version control in an SOP is important because it allows the team to:
options: Identify the approved procedure used at each session
Guarantee improvement after every protocol change
Replace assessor training with a document number
Remove the need to record deviations in testing
explanation: Version control identifies which approved procedure was used at each session and helps trace later differences.

text: Two assessors administer the same flexibility test. The SOP should reduce variation by specifying:
options: The athlete’s preferred result and expected ranking
Which assessor may ignore the athlete’s pain report
The instructions, position, endpoint, and scoring rule
A different scoring scale for each independent assessor
explanation: Shared instructions, position, endpoint, and scoring rule reduce assessor-dependent variation in the flexibility test.

text: An SOP cannot replace which professional responsibilities?
options: Record the assessment time in the approved SOP
Follow the approved warm-up in every session
Use clinical judgment, consent, and safety
Use the specified equipment model consistently
explanation: An SOP standardizes procedures but cannot replace professional judgment, informed consent, or safety responsibilities.

text: When testing athletes who speak different languages, standardization is best supported by:
options: Allow athletes to interpret unfamiliar instructions independently
Remove all verbal instructions from the standard protocol
Change the scoring rule for each language group tested
Use an approved translated script and check understanding
explanation: An approved translated script and a check of understanding preserve the intended instructions across language groups.

text: A routine SOP audit should compare observed practice with:
options: The current approved procedure and its safety requirements
The athlete’s predicted competition result in the SOP
The most favourable historical score in the SOP
The coach’s preferred reporting style only in the SOP
explanation: An SOP audit compares observed practice with the current approved procedure and its safety requirements.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, before a maximal exercise test, the practitioner should first verify:
options: that screening covers contraindications, preparation, and emergency procedures
that history, medication, and symptoms are reviewed without readiness checks
that prior scores and coach expectations replace formal screening
that staff and equipment eliminate the need to check contraindications
explanation: Pre-test safety requires screening, preparation instructions, contraindication review, and emergency readiness.

text: An athlete reports new chest pressure during the preparation for a maximal treadmill test. Before proceeding, the practitioner should verify:
options: That the athlete can continue if the coach accepts the risk
That screening, deferral, and emergency readiness are confirmed
That a previous normal test overrides today’s new symptom
That today’s symptom is omitted to protect the schedule
explanation: New chest pressure is a safety concern; the practitioner must confirm appropriate deferral and emergency readiness before any maximal test.

text: An athlete has started a medication that may alter heart-rate response. Before a graded test, verify:
options: That the medication can be ignored if the athlete feels motivated
That the old heart-rate zones are used without adjustment
That medication, symptoms, and safety readiness are reviewed
That the coach’s expected score determines test readiness
explanation: Medication can alter heart-rate response, so medication history, symptoms, and safety readiness must be reviewed before grading the test.

text: A small testing venue has no trained emergency responder present. Before a maximal test, verify:
options: That the athlete signs a form accepting all responsibility
That the test is shortened without changing the safety plan
That a high previous score indicates low current risk
That trained staff, equipment, and emergency procedures are ready
explanation: A maximal test requires trained staff, suitable equipment, and ready emergency procedures before it begins.

text: An athlete arrives after an overnight shift and has not followed the required pre-test instructions. Before testing, verify:
options: That readiness is reviewed and testing is postponed or modified if needed
That the athlete’s motivation compensates for non-standard preparation
That the result can be compared with a rested athlete without adjustment
That the deviation is ignored if the session is already scheduled
explanation: Overnight work and non-standard preparation may compromise readiness, so testing should be reviewed and postponed or modified when necessary.

text: An athlete has fever and marked fatigue on the day of a maximal test. Before proceeding, verify:
options: That the athlete can complete a slower test without further review
That fever and fatigue prompt deferral and clinical guidance
That only the final score is recorded despite fever and fatigue
That a warm-up alone determines safety despite fever and fatigue
explanation: Fever and marked fatigue are acute safety concerns; symptoms should be assessed, testing deferred if needed, and clinical guidance obtained.

text: A 15-year-old is scheduled for a maximal assessment but the required consent process is incomplete. Before testing, verify:
options: That coach permission alone replaces required consent for a maximal test
That previous participation counts as current consent for this assessment
Required consent/assent, screening, and safety arrangements are complete
That anonymous results remove the need for permission from the minor
explanation: A minor's maximal assessment should proceed only after the applicable consent/assent process, screening, and safety arrangements are complete.

text: A hot, humid environment is planned for an exhaustive test. Before proceeding, verify:
options: That hydration and emergency planning are unnecessary for fit athletes
That the same workload is safe regardless of heat exposure
That stopping rules can be relaxed to obtain a complete score
That heat risk, hydration, monitoring, and stopping rules suffice
explanation: Heat and humidity increase risk, so hydration, monitoring, staffing, and stopping procedures must be adequate before exhaustive testing.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, instrument calibration is performed to:
options: Check measurement accuracy against a known standard
Confirm that the athlete understands the measurement task
Change the test construct to match the equipment
Replace repeated recordings with a single reading
explanation: Calibration checks whether the instrument produces accurate readings relative to a known reference.

text: Before a force-plate session, the operator applies a known load and checks the displayed value. This is:
options: A test of the athlete’s motivation
Calibration against a known standard
A replacement for data cleaning
A change to the measured construct
explanation: Applying a known load and checking the displayed value compares the instrument with a known standard, which is calibration.

text: A metabolic cart shows increasing error during a quality check. The most appropriate response is to:
options: Continue testing and correct values later without documentation
Change the athlete’s expected oxygen uptake for the device
Investigate, service or recalibrate the device, and document it
Use the highest previous result as the current measurement
explanation: Increasing device error requires investigation and service or recalibration, with the action documented before further testing.

text: A calibrated scale is placed on an uneven surface. The main concern is that:
options: Calibration makes positioning irrelevant for the device
The athlete’s age changes the scale response for the device
Setup can introduce measurement error despite prior calibration
A single reading is more valid than repeated readings
explanation: An uneven setup can introduce measurement error even when the scale was previously calibrated.

text: The date, reference standard, result, and operator should be recorded after calibration mainly to:
options: Predict the athlete’s competition ranking
Replace the instrument manual for this device
Make every later score identical across sessions
Provide traceability for the measurement system
explanation: Recording the date, standard, result, and operator creates traceability for the measurement system and its calibration status.

text: If a timing gate fails its pre-session accuracy check, the team should:
options: Use the device because the athlete is already warmed up
Estimate times from the athlete’s previous ranking
Remove the gate from service until the problem is resolved
Round every result to hide the device error
explanation: A timing gate that fails its accuracy check should be removed from service until the fault is resolved.

text: Zeroing a sensor before a trial primarily establishes:
options: The athlete’s maximal performance capacity with the same protocol
The baseline reference from which the measurement is read
The validity of the entire test construct for the device
The appropriate normative percentile for the device
explanation: Zeroing establishes the baseline reference from which subsequent sensor readings are measured.

text: Calibration improves measurement quality most directly by reducing:
options: The need for informed consent for the device
The effect of athlete motivation for the device
The importance of standardizing instructions
Systematic measurement error from the instrument
explanation: Calibration most directly reduces systematic error introduced by the instrument, not athlete motivation or consent requirements.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a quality-control log is useful because it records:
options: The athlete's predicted ranking before data collection began
The coach's preferred target score and selection expectation
The report layout and font used for presenting results
Equipment checks, deviations, maintenance, and corrective actions
explanation: Quality-control records help identify procedural deviations and maintain traceability.

text: A quality-control log shows that a timing gate was moved between sessions. Its main value is to:
options: Prove that the faster session reflects adaptation
Record a procedural deviation that may affect comparability
Replace the need for a timing check in the quality record
Determine the athlete’s selection status in the quality record
explanation: Recording that the gate moved documents a procedural deviation that may explain differences in session comparability.

text: A maintenance log for a metabolic analyser should include:
options: The coach’s preferred athlete ranking in the quality record
Only the best oxygen-uptake value obtained in the quality record
Service dates, actions performed, and relevant equipment status
The athlete’s predicted response before testing in the quality record
explanation: A maintenance log should record service dates, work performed, and the analyser’s relevant equipment status.

text: An audit finds that recovery intervals were shorter than specified for three athletes. The report should:
options: Delete those athletes without recording why in the quality record
Document the deviation and qualify or repeat the result
Treat the scores as automatically equivalent to standard tests
Change the recovery interval in the original SOP without approval
explanation: Short recovery intervals can alter performance; the deviation should be documented and the results qualified or repeated.

text: A traceable data record should link an athlete’s result with:
options: Only the final score and coach comment in the quality record
The athlete’s ranking in a previous season in the quality record
Date, protocol version, equipment status, assessor, and conditions
A preferred normative percentile in the quality record
explanation: A traceable result links the score to its date, protocol version, equipment status, assessor, and testing conditions.

text: A corrective action in a testing quality system is intended to:
options: Make an unexpected result match the prediction in the quality record
Remove all low scores from the dataset in the quality record
Address the cause of a detected problem and prevent recurrence
Allow protocol changes without documentation in the quality record
explanation: Corrective action addresses the cause of a detected problem and reduces the chance that it will recur.

text: A quality-control review notices missing warm-up records. The immediate reporting decision should be to:
options: Assume the warm-up was identical for everyone in the quality record
Fill the fields using the athlete’s best previous session
Flag the missing information and qualify the interpretation
Ignore the omission because warm-up never affects performance
explanation: Missing warm-up records create uncertainty, so they should be flagged and the interpretation qualified rather than fabricated.

text: The main purpose of periodically reviewing quality-control logs is to:
options: Increase every athlete’s score in the quality record
Replace the need for staff competency checks in the quality record
Select the most convenient test for the coach in the quality record
Identify recurring process problems and improve data integrity
explanation: Periodic review identifies recurring process problems and supports improvements in data integrity.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, informed consent means that the athlete receives information about:
options: The procedure, expected score, and schedule without discussing possible risks
The likely benefits and coach recommendation without describing voluntary choice
The opinions of staff and teammates about the athlete's readiness and selection
The procedure, risks, benefits, voluntary choice, data use, and how to withdraw
explanation: Valid consent explains the procedure, risks, benefits, voluntary choice, data use, and withdrawal process before testing.

text: Before an athlete consents to a blood-lactate assessment, the information should include:
options: Only the expected performance benefit before consent
The procedure, risks, benefits, alternatives, and free choice
The coach’s decision about whether participation is compulsory
The athlete’s predicted score and selection probability
explanation: Before blood-lactate testing, the athlete should understand the procedure, risks, benefits, alternatives, and freedom to decline.

text: An athlete agrees to testing only after being told selection will depend on participation. The main consent concern is:
options: The equipment calibration date before consent
The athlete’s normative percentile before consent
Whether the report uses a graph or table
Whether consent was voluntary and unpressured
explanation: Linking participation to selection can undermine free choice, so the team must assess whether consent was voluntary and unpressured.

text: A testing form states that samples will be stored for future research but does not explain who may access them. The team should:
options: Clarify purpose, access, storage, and withdrawal
Collect the sample because storage is implied
Ask teammates whether the use is acceptable
Release identifiable data to the sponsor by default
explanation: Future research storage requires a clear purpose, access rules, storage arrangements, and a withdrawal process before samples or data are retained.

text: An athlete withdraws consent halfway through a non-therapeutic testing session. The practitioner should:
options: Continue because the first signature remains valid
Stop and explain how collected data will be handled
Ask the coach to overrule the athlete
Record a non-compliance penalty for withdrawal
explanation: Withdrawal ends participation; the practitioner should stop and explain how data already collected will be handled.

text: To support valid consent for a complex testing protocol, the practitioner should:
options: Invite questions and confirm understanding
Use technical language without checking comprehension
Provide only the schedule because risks are obvious
Ask for agreement before explaining the procedure
explanation: Inviting questions and checking understanding helps ensure that agreement is informed rather than merely signed.

text: For a minor participating in performance testing, the consent process should follow:
options: The coach’s verbal instruction alone before consent
The same process as an anonymous adult survey in every setting
Required guardian permission and the young athlete’s assent
A decision made by the strongest athlete on the team
explanation: Minor participation requires the applicable guardian permission together with the young athlete’s assent.

text: A protocol changes from non-invasive movement testing to venous blood sampling. Before continuing, the team should:
options: Treat the original consent as covering every future procedure
Explain the material change and obtain amended consent
Proceed if the expected score is important to selection
Ask only the data analyst whether the change is acceptable
explanation: Venous blood sampling is a material change from movement testing, so it requires explanation and amended consent before continuing.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, confidentiality in athlete testing primarily concerns:
options: Give the coach unrestricted access to identifiable raw results by default
Tell teammates about results when selection decisions depend on them directly
Store identifiable data without access controls if the report is internal
Prevent inappropriate disclosure of identifiable athlete data without consent
explanation: Confidentiality protects identifiable information while allowing appropriate, consented professional communication.

text: A performance report is shared with a strength coach. The most appropriate access arrangement is:
options: Role-based access to necessary identifiable information
Open access to all raw data for every staff member
Public posting because the athlete is on a team
Unrestricted forwarding to sponsors and teammates
explanation: Role-based access gives the strength coach only the identifiable information needed for an authorized professional purpose.

text: A presentation to the coaching group is based on injury-screening data. To reduce disclosure risk, the practitioner should:
options: Use identifiable examples to make the presentation memorable
Send the complete raw spreadsheet to every attendee
Include names because the data were collected at work
Use aggregated or de-identified results unless authorized
explanation: Aggregated or de-identified results reduce disclosure risk when individual identity is not necessary for the coaching presentation.

text: Raw testing data are transferred to a consultant. The safest routine is to:
options: Use a personal messaging account for speed
Remove the access log so transfer remains private
Use an approved secure channel and share authorized data
Send identifiable data without checking authorization
explanation: An approved secure channel and authorized data scope protect raw testing information during transfer to a consultant.

text: A coach requests an athlete’s identifiable pain and test results without the athlete’s agreed data-sharing permission. The practitioner should first:
options: Clarify authorization, purpose, and data needed
Release all results because the coach supervises training
Send results to teammates for corroboration
Delete the record to avoid the conversation
explanation: Before sharing identifiable pain and test results, the practitioner should confirm authorization, purpose, and the minimum data needed.

text: A spreadsheet containing identifiable test results is accidentally emailed to the wrong recipient. The appropriate first response is to:
options: Follow the breach procedure, contain disclosure, and document it
Ignore the incident if the recipient is another professional
Alter the original record so the mistake cannot be found
Announce the athlete’s result to the team for transparency
explanation: An accidental disclosure requires the breach procedure, immediate containment, and documentation so the incident can be managed and reviewed.

text: A testing programme sets a retention period for identifiable records. This supports confidentiality by:
options: Keep every record indefinitely for convenience
Define secure retention and disposal for the purpose
Allow any staff member to copy data before deletion
Replace access controls with a retention period
explanation: A defined retention and disposal period limits how long identifiable records remain accessible for the stated purpose.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a pre-test contraindication should generally lead the practitioner to:
options: Continue after documenting symptoms if requested
Complete at reduced intensity without clinical review
Defer or modify testing and seek clinical guidance
Exclude symptoms from the report to avoid bias
explanation: Contraindications are safety signals requiring appropriate deferral, modification, or medical review.

text: An athlete reports faintness while seated before an exercise test. The practitioner should:
options: Pause testing and seek appropriate clinical guidance
Proceed at lower intensity without clinical review
Record symptoms after completing the test
Ask the athlete to conceal symptoms from staff
explanation: Faintness before exercise testing warrants pausing the test and obtaining appropriate clinical guidance rather than proceeding.

text: An athlete with fever requests a maximal test because selection trials are near. The safest action is to:
options: Proceed if the athlete signs a waiver accepting risk
Postpone testing until the acute illness resolves
Replace safety screening with a longer warm-up
Use the previous score as today’s result without testing
explanation: Fever indicates acute illness, so maximal testing should be postponed until the illness resolves.

text: A pre-test blood-pressure reading is markedly above the service’s safety threshold. The practitioner should:
options: Confirm the reading and follow the referral or deferral procedure
Continue because the athlete is asymptomatic before testing
Delete the value because it may lower the athlete’s ranking
Use a harder warm-up to normalize the reading before testing
explanation: A markedly high blood-pressure reading should be confirmed and handled under the service’s referral or deferral procedure.

text: An athlete describes new exertional chest pain during screening. The practitioner should:
options: Proceed with a shorter maximal test
Record pain only if it returns during testing
Ask the coach to judge whether pain is serious
Defer testing and arrange medical evaluation
explanation: New exertional chest pain is a red flag requiring test deferral and medical evaluation.

text: An athlete presents with severe sleep loss and dizziness before a maximal test. The practitioner should:
options: Assess readiness and modify or defer testing for safety
Treat the planned schedule as more important than readiness
Allow maximal effort but shorten the report afterward
Compare the result only with rested athletes
explanation: Severe sleep loss with dizziness may compromise readiness and safety, so testing should be assessed and modified or deferred.

text: An athlete reports a recent medication change before a heart-rate-based test. The practitioner should:
options: Ignore the change because medication cannot affect exercise response
Review the change and adapt the protocol or interpretation
Use the old heart-rate zones without any qualification
Ask the athlete to stop prescribed medication before testing
explanation: Medication changes can alter heart-rate responses, so the protocol and interpretation should be adapted after reviewing the change.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, to improve repeated field-test reliability, the team should standardize:
options: Only the stopwatch and assessor need to be standardized
Instructions, warm-up, equipment, surface, timing, and setting
The athlete may choose a different warm-up and footwear each time
Timing can be adjusted to match the expected score
explanation: Standardized instructions, warm-up, equipment, surface, timing, and setting reduce avoidable variation in repeated field tests.

text: For repeated 20-m sprint testing, which condition should be kept constant whenever feasible?
options: The athlete’s preferred result across sessions
The amount of fatigue accumulated before testing
The coach’s prediction of the next score
Surface, footwear, start, timing, and instructions
explanation: Keeping surface, footwear, start, timing, and instructions constant makes repeated 20-m sprint scores more comparable.

text: For serial blood-lactate measurements, reliability is improved by standardizing:
options: Only the athlete’s body mass across sessions
Sampling site, workload, timing, and analyser method
The reported value after seeing the previous result
A different stage duration for every session
explanation: Sampling site, workload, timing, and analyser method must be consistent to compare serial blood-lactate measurements.

text: A countermovement-jump protocol is being repeated across a season. The instructions should specify:
options: That athletes may choose a different technique at each assessment
That only the highest athlete score is retained across sessions
Whether arm movement, depth, attempts, rest, and scoring are permitted
That rest is shortened when the first score is low across sessions
explanation: Specifying arm movement, depth, attempts, rest, and scoring makes repeated countermovement-jump results comparable.

text: To compare morning and afternoon readiness scores, the team should record and standardize relevant factors such as:
options: Only the athlete’s jersey number and team
The coach’s expected improvement and ranking
A different device and timing at each session
Recent food, fluid, sleep, exercise, and time of day
explanation: Food, fluid, sleep, exercise, and time of day can affect readiness, so these factors should be recorded and standardized where feasible.

text: A repeated flexibility test is administered by several assessors. The most important standardization step is to:
options: Allow each assessor to choose the movement endpoint
Use the most favourable reading as the reference
Change measurement units between assessors
Use a shared endpoint, script, and recording rule
explanation: A shared movement endpoint, script, and recording rule reduces differences between flexibility assessors.

text: To compare a field test across a training block, the team should:
options: Keep timing, equipment, preparation, and conditions comparable
Use different warm-ups and recovery periods at every testing session
Use a harder surface for the second field assessment session
Choose the final scoring rule after reviewing all results
explanation: Comparable timing, equipment, preparation, and conditions are needed to interpret field-test changes across a training block.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a test administrator should stop an exercise test when:
options: the administrator waits for the test to reach a maximal score
the administrator observes a termination criterion or concerning symptom
the administrator continues despite a warning sign if the athlete wishes
the administrator stops at a fixed time despite symptoms or protocol
explanation: The administrator should stop when a predefined termination criterion or concerning symptom appears, protecting the athlete before a maximal score is reached.

text: During a graded test, an athlete develops crushing chest pain. The administrator should stop the test when:
options: The planned maximal stage is reached during testing
The athlete says the symptom is tolerable during testing
The symptom appears and the termination procedure is activated
The scheduled test duration has elapsed during testing
explanation: Crushing chest pain is an immediate termination signal, so the test should stop and the safety procedure should be activated.

text: An exercise-test monitor shows a concerning rhythm change. The administrator should:
options: Continue until the athlete reaches the target score
Wait for the next stage to see whether it resolves
Ignore it if the athlete wants the result recorded
Stop the test and follow the defined emergency procedure
explanation: A concerning rhythm change can threaten safety and requires immediate termination followed by the defined emergency procedure.

text: An athlete becomes confused and loses coordination during an exhaustive test. The administrator should:
options: Stop when confusion or loss of coordination appears
Continue until the planned workload is complete
Continue because selection depends on the score
Continue if the athlete requests another stage
explanation: Confusion or loss of coordination signals that the athlete cannot safely continue, so the test should stop immediately.

text: During a cycle test, an athlete develops severe dizziness and cannot maintain cadence. The administrator should:
options: Continue until the planned workload is complete
Stop the test and follow the safety procedure
Continue if the athlete says symptoms are tolerable
Record the symptom while keeping the trial running
explanation: A new severe symptom or loss of control requires test termination and a safety assessment.

text: During an incremental test, an athlete develops severe dyspnoea and an unsafe oxygen-saturation response. The correct action is to:
options: Continue until the next workload stage for completeness
Record the symptom but allow the athlete to decide alone
Terminate the test and start the safety procedure
Stop only when the planned time has been reached
explanation: Severe dyspnoea with an unsafe oxygen-saturation response meets safety criteria for termination and initiation of the safety procedure.

text: The timing gate fails while an athlete is running at speed. The administrator should:
options: Continue because equipment faults cannot affect safety
Estimate the result from the previous season
Repeat immediately without checking the device
Stop if equipment failure threatens safety or validity
explanation: Equipment failure can compromise both safety and validity, so the run should stop when the fault threatens either.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a good test report should communicate results in a way that is:
options: Raw and uninterpreted, leaving context to the reader
Selective, emphasizing the best result while omitting uncertainty
Technical and audience-insensitive, using unexplained terminology
Accurate, clear, contextualized, and relevant to the decision
explanation: A useful report states the result accurately, adds context, and explains its relevance to the decision in language the audience can use.

text: A report compares an athlete’s current sprint time with baseline. The most useful presentation includes:
options: Only the current raw value without the baseline for a training decision
The change, error or uncertainty, conditions, and practical context
The best historical value while omitting unsuccessful trials
A technical statistic without explaining its decision relevance
explanation: Comparing current sprint time with baseline is most useful when the report includes the change, uncertainty, conditions, and practical context.

text: A coach asks whether a small improvement is enough to change training. The report should:
options: State the result without reference to error or the decision threshold
Relate the change to error, worthwhile change, and the decision
Describe the athlete as fully recovered regardless of the evidence
Replace the measurement with the coach’s expectation for a training decision
explanation: A small improvement should be compared with measurement error, the worthwhile-change threshold, and the decision before training is changed.

text: When a test result is uncertain because preparation differed from baseline, the report should:
options: Hide the deviation to make the report concise
Assume the difference represents adaptation
Mention the deviation and qualify the comparison
Use technical language to remove uncertainty
explanation: Different preparation makes the comparison uncertain, so the report should disclose the deviation and qualify the interpretation.

text: A report for a multidisciplinary team should:
options: Use unexplained abbreviations to demonstrate expertise
Report only the most favourable interpretation
Remove context so each discipline decides independently
Explain results in language suited to the audience
explanation: A multidisciplinary report should explain results in language appropriate to its audience rather than rely on unexplained technical terms.

text: An athlete receives a personal testing report. The clearest format is one that:
options: Explains the measure, result, uncertainty, and next step clearly
Lists raw scores without definitions for a training decision
Uses group rankings as a diagnosis for a training decision
Omits limitations to preserve motivation for a training decision
explanation: An athlete-facing report should define the measure, state the result and uncertainty, and identify a clear next step.

text: A report recommends changing training based on one unexpected score. Before making that recommendation, it should:
options: Consider protocol quality, repeatability, context, and other evidence
Treat the single score as definitive for a training decision
Use the most dramatic explanation available for a training decision
Ignore the athlete’s symptoms and goals for a training decision
explanation: One unexpected score should be checked against protocol quality, repeatability, context, symptoms, and other evidence before training changes are recommended.
